title: Wang Bi lesson (video, full 3:48), structure as code
alt: A green terminal teaches how Wang Bi read a hexagram: positions, centres, answering lines and the master line, built one part at a time.

platforms.x:
Wang Bi (226–249) died at 23. His I-Ching commentary was the official one from the Tang until Zhu Xi's replaced it in 1313. His method reads a hexagram as a data structure.

Han scholars read each hexagram through a web of correspondences: seasons, stars, the five phases, trigrams nested inside trigrams. Wang Bi dropped the web. His rule, 得意忘象: once you have the meaning, let go of the image.

What he kept is structure. Six lines, each yang or yin, read by position:

Lines 2 to 5 hold rank. Lines 1 and 6 are the start and the end.
A yang line sits correctly in an odd place, a yin line in an even one.
Lines 2 and 5 are the centres of the lower and upper trigram.
1 answers 4, 2 answers 5, 3 answers 6, but only when one is yin and the other yang.
When one line differs from the other five, it rules the hexagram. His phrase: the few rule the many.

An index, a parity check, a pairwise XOR, a count. Anyone can run it on any of the 64 and get the same answer. That is why Six Lines is built on it.

The Qing imperial catalog summed him up in one line: he threw out the image-numbers and explained the text with Laozi and Zhuangzi. We keep the first half.

> popcount(師 Army) == 1 # one yang rules five yin

A 4-minute lesson in reading a hexagram his way, made for @sixlinesapp → sixlines.day
